# Open Forge in this project

**You may delete this page.** It is a guide for the people who run this project, and it describes the file formats agents follow when they write workspace files. Everything here is also in `open-forge help concepts`, so no rule depends on this page. To keep it deleted through `open-forge update`, add `.agents/README.md` to `removedFiles` in `.agents/open-forge.json`.

Open Forge tells agents where your rules and knowledge live. You decide what they use with the list under `## Entries` in [loader.md](loader.md). Every file here is yours, and everything works without the CLI. The CLI's settings and ownership files support maintenance and give agents no authority.

## Choose the context folder

At first installation, `open-forge install --main-root <folder>` chooses the context folder. The default is `--main-root .agents`. A custom folder, such as `docs/context`, must be absent or empty. Interactive Install asks `Where should Open Forge keep its context files?` when the flag is omitted.

The loader, this guide and ordinary categories live in the context folder. Native Skills stay in `.agents/skills/`, settings in `.agents/open-forge.json`, and ownership in `.agents/open-forge.lock.json`. New settings use schema version 4 for every layout. Workspace-root `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` point to the selected loader.

Use `./...` for an exact workspace-relative CLI path. Short source IDs, such as `memory/crystallized`, work with either layout. Older CLIs do not support custom roots. Relocating an established installation is not available yet, including through `install --configure`. Editing `mainRoot` in settings moves no files.

Default installation preview:

```sh
open-forge install --preset essentials --dry-run
```

Custom context folder preview:

```sh
open-forge install --preset essentials --main-root docs/context --dry-run
```

Review the plan, then repeat the chosen request without `--dry-run` and with `--automatic` to apply it unattended.

## Use a document you already have

Your rules may already live somewhere, such as a contribution guide. Include it where it is:

```sh
open-forge route include CONTRIBUTING.md --description "Contribution rules to follow" --tag LoadNow
```

That adds this line to the loader, which you can also write by hand:

```markdown
- [Contribution rules to follow](../CONTRIBUTING.md) - #LoadNow
```

`#LoadNow` means agents read it before every task. Leave the tag off when agents should open the file only when its description fits the task. To limit a file to some work, add a pattern: `--apply-to "**/*.cs"` writes `- applies to` and the pattern at the end of the line.

Any text file works, including rules you wrote for other tools, such as `.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. Open Forge ignores another tool's frontmatter and activation settings, so the line's tags and conditions decide when agents read the file. Include files one by one rather than whole folders. A Markdown file with its own `## Entries` list, such as `docs/team/_team.md`, brings its listed files along.

Including a file asks agents to read it. It doesn't make its claims accepted and doesn't let agents edit it. `open-forge route exclude CONTRIBUTING.md` removes the line and leaves the file alone.

## Write your first rule

The rules that matter most are the ones only your project knows. Write them down as Directives, one subject per file:

```sh
open-forge route create directives/exports --description "How data exports are formatted" --tag LoadNow --tag Directive
```

Then write the rule under `## Instructions`, as [Rule files](#rule-files) shows. Start with one rule that agents keep getting wrong, and add more as you notice them. This is your framework: rename, restructure and replace anything here to fit how your team works.

## Add only what helps

Each folder holds one kind of content, and you add only the ones you want:

- **Directives** hold rules agents must follow.
- **Memory** holds notes that help work continue. Its states hold accepted knowledge (Crystallized), work in progress (Working), findings not accepted yet (Emerging) and history (Archived).
- **Guidance** offers advice for recurring choices.
- **Patterns** show reusable shapes for code and documents.
- **Templates** provide starting files to copy.
- **Maps** point to important sources.
- **Skills** expose capabilities through native `SKILL.md` packages.

Existing ADRs and docs can stay where they are and be included. Named record kinds and workflows come from Extensions.

`open-forge install --configure` adds or leaves out these parts later, and `open-forge route init <category> --framework` restores one.

## Stop using something

Remove its line from the loader, or run `open-forge route exclude` with its catalogue, such as `.agents/patterns/_patterns.md`. Agents stop using the whole branch, and its files stay as notes. Remove or replace any part that depends on it first. Your accepted requirements, and instructions your agent tool loads on its own, still apply.

Inside a catalogue, the list follows the files on disk. To keep a file as a note there, move it out of the routed folder and remove its line. To get rid of it, delete the file and its line. When the CLI manages updates, record the removal too, so updates don't bring it back. Custom's `remove` choice only stops Open Forge managing the defaults. It keeps existing files and routes, and it doesn't switch them off.

## Reuse your knowledge elsewhere

When your rules prove useful, share them:

- **Include** uses a document already in this project, where it lives.
- A **Library** projects a folder registered in this workspace into another place through links.
- An **Extension** packages files you can install in any project.

## Find the details

- [loader.md](loader.md) says what agents read and how they use it.
- `open-forge help concepts` explains every concept in one place, including the file formats below.
- `open-forge <command> --help` shows a command's options.
- The website has the full guide: <https://thelithiumforge.github.io/open-forge/>.

## Writing workspace files

Read this before you write or change workspace context: catalogues, rule files, metadata or lines under `Entries`. It describes the file shapes that agents and the Open Forge CLI both read. A file in another shape is ignored or reported as malformed. This section describes formats, not how to do your work.

### Lines under Entries

Each entry is one line:

```markdown
- [C# rules to follow when changing C# code](csharp/_csharp.md) - #Directive #KeepInMind - applies to `**/*.cs`, `**/*.csproj`
```

- The link text is the description. Write it so a reader can decide whether to open the file.
- The path is relative to the file that holds the list. In the loader it can leave the folder, such as `../CONTRIBUTING.md`.
- Tags come after ` - `, each with `#`. Only #LoadNow and #KeepInMind change loading. Leave them off when the file should be opened only when its description fits the task.
- Conditions come last, as `applies to` followed by patterns in backticks, separated by a comma and a space. For a file in `.agents/`, they repeat the `applyTo` patterns in its frontmatter. For a file outside `.agents/`, the line is where they are set.

Keep each entry's path, description, tags and conditions current. With the CLI, preview `open-forge index --dry-run`, then run `open-forge index`. Without it, update the lines by hand.

### Catalogues

A catalogue lists a folder's context under its own `## Entries`. A folder has one, named `_{folder-name}.md`. The older names `index.md`, `_index.md`, `references.md` and `_references.md` also work.

```markdown
---
open-forge:
  description: Rules for testing, read before changing tests
  tags: [Directive, Testing]
---

# Testing

## What rules apply to tests?

Rules that apply to every test in this repository.

## Axioms

- inherited - No local axioms; loaded ancestor axioms remain active.

## Entries

- [How to name and place tests](naming.md) - #Directive
```

- Under the title, write the one question the folder answers as a `##` heading, then a short paragraph on what the folder holds. A catalogue describes its own folder and does not name other routes.
- Put rules for everything below the catalogue under `## Axioms`. A catalogue without rules of its own has only the `inherited` line shown above. A missing or empty Axioms section also adds no rules. Never mix that line with local rules.
- List the folder's files and the catalogues of its child folders under `## Entries`. An empty list is valid.

### Rule files

A rule file, such as a Directive, puts its rules under a non-empty `## Instructions` section. They apply within the scope the file states.

```markdown
---
open-forge:
  description: Run the full test suite before you hand off a change
  tags: [Directive, Testing]
---

# Test before handoff

## Instructions

- Run the full test suite before you hand off a change, and report any failure with its output.
```

### Metadata

New routed files in `.agents/` start with YAML frontmatter:

- `description` is required. It helps readers decide whether to open the file.
- `tags` is required. Write tag names without `#`.
- `applyTo` is optional. It holds glob patterns, as a list or a comma-separated string, that limit when the file applies.
- `responsibility` is optional. It says what the file defines, so an editor knows what belongs there. It adds no authority.

Follow the `frontmatter` setting in `.agents/open-forge.json`. `root` puts the fields at the top level, and `scoped` puts them under `open-forge:`, as in the examples above. A missing setting means scoped. Keep all Open Forge fields together. Both forms of `applyTo` are read. Equal pattern sets count once, and different sets are invalid.

A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata. A file outside `.agents/` that the loader lists needs no frontmatter, because its line carries the description, tags and conditions.

### Where things go

- Connect related material with relative links to local sources and precise references. Reuse consistent descriptive tags for shared subjects. Add links and tags only when they help someone find or retrieve something.
- Put detail in the narrowest source that defines it. A parent catalogue keeps only the summary and link needed to choose that source. Put material at workspace level only when it applies across the workspace. Don't repeat inherited rules.
- A scope is a folder that narrows everything after it. Scopes can nest before, between or after deeper route segments. A scope holds only the routes that are useful there, and doesn't need to copy another scope or the installed defaults.

For example, a C# scope might hold a #LoadNow design file and an on-demand Windows scope. Selecting C# loads its design file. A #LoadNow file under Windows loads only once Windows is selected.

### Changes that survive updates

Updates can replace direct edits to shipped files. For a change that should survive them, write `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the file. It is read right after its base and wins only where the two say different things about the same content. Review the update plan before you apply it.

### Terms

- A **route** is a path through catalogues and Entries. A **root route** is a line in the loader.
- A **slug** is a concrete folder name in a route.
- **#Core** labels base routing, loading, workspace orientation and reusable agent-facing roles.
- **#Memory** labels self-growing Markdown state for active work, coordination, accepted knowledge, candidates and history.
- **#Extension** labels optional packaged routes, capabilities, integrations and support files.

These labels add nothing to what agents read and don't make Open Forge manage a file.

- Tags come after ` - `, each with `#`. Only #LoadNow and #KeepInMind change loading. Leave them off when the file should be opened only when its description fits the task.
- Conditions come last, as `applies to` followed by patterns in backticks, separated by a comma and a space. For a file in `.agents/`, they repeat the `applyTo` patterns in its frontmatter. For a file outside `.agents/`, the line is where they are set.

Keep each entry's path, description, tags and conditions current. With the CLI, preview `open-forge index --dry-run`, then run `open-forge index`. Without it, update the lines by hand.

### Catalogues

A catalogue lists a folder's context under its own `## Entries`. A folder has one, named `_{folder-name}.md`. The older names `index.md`, `_index.md`, `references.md` and `_references.md` also work.

```markdown
---
open-forge:
  description: Rules for testing, read before changing tests
  tags: [Directive, Testing]
---

# Testing

## What rules apply to tests?

Rules that apply to every test in this repository.

## Axioms

- inherited - No local axioms; loaded ancestor axioms remain active.

## Entries

- [How to name and place tests](naming.md) - #Directive
```

- Under the title, write the one question the folder answers as a `##` heading, then a short paragraph on what the folder holds. A catalogue describes its own folder and does not name other routes.
- Put rules for everything below the catalogue under `## Axioms`. A catalogue without rules of its own has only the `inherited` line shown above. A missing or empty Axioms section also adds no rules. Never mix that line with local rules.
- List the folder's files and the catalogues of its child folders under `## Entries`. An empty list is valid.

### Rule files

A rule file, such as a Directive, puts its rules under a non-empty `## Instructions` section. They apply within the scope the file states.

```markdown
---
open-forge:
  description: Run the full test suite before you hand off a change
  tags: [Directive, Testing]
---

# Test before handoff

## Instructions

- Run the full test suite before you hand off a change, and report any failure with its output.
```

### Metadata

New routed files in `.agents/` start with YAML frontmatter:

- `description` is required. It helps readers decide whether to open the file.
- `tags` is required. Write tag names without `#`.
- `applyTo` is optional. It holds glob patterns, as a list or a comma-separated string, that limit when the file applies.
- `responsibility` is optional. It says what the file defines, so an editor knows what belongs there. It adds no authority.

Follow the `frontmatter` setting in `.agents/open-forge.json`. `root` puts the fields at the top level, and `scoped` puts them under `open-forge:`, as in the examples above. A missing setting means scoped. Keep all Open Forge fields together. Both forms of `applyTo` are read. Equal pattern sets count once, and different sets are invalid.

A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata. A file outside `.agents/` that the loader lists needs no frontmatter, because its line carries the description, tags and conditions.

### Where things go

- Connect related material with relative links to local sources and precise references. Reuse consistent descriptive tags for shared subjects. Add links and tags only when they help someone find or retrieve something.
- Put detail in the narrowest source that defines it. A parent catalogue keeps only the summary and link needed to choose that source. Put material at workspace level only when it applies across the workspace. Don't repeat inherited rules.
- A scope is a folder that narrows everything after it. Scopes can nest before, between or after deeper route segments. A scope holds only the routes that are useful there, and doesn't need to copy another scope or the installed defaults.

For example, a C# scope might hold a #LoadNow design file and an on-demand Windows scope. Selecting C# loads its design file. A #LoadNow file under Windows loads only once Windows is selected.

### Changes that survive updates

Updates can replace direct edits to shipped files. For a change that should survive them, write `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the file. It is read right after its base and wins only where the two say different things about the same content. Review the update plan before you apply it.

### Terms

- A **route** is a path through catalogues and Entries. A **root route** is a line in the loader.
- A **slug** is a concrete folder name in a route.
- **#Core** labels base routing, loading, workspace orientation and reusable agent-facing roles.
- **#Memory** labels self-growing Markdown state for active work, coordination, accepted knowledge, candidates and history.
- **#Extension** labels optional packaged routes, capabilities, integrations and support files.

These labels add nothing to what agents read and don't make Open Forge manage a file.

open-forge:

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.
- Within the authority granted for the work, add an ordinary record or scoped route when needed. Ask when placement would change accepted meaning or cross an unresolved authority boundary. Get explicit user direction before creating a new top-level Memory state.

## Entries

- [Useful history that no longer controls current work](archived/_archived.md) - #Memory #Archived #Contextual #Historical
- [Accepted knowledge that should remain current](crystallized/_crystallized.md) - #LoadNow #Memory #Crystallized #CurrentTruth
- [Useful material that is not accepted yet](emerging/_emerging.md) - #KeepInMind #Memory #Emerging #Contextual #Candidate
- [Temporary memory that helps agents continue or resume active work](working/_working.md) - #LoadNow #Memory #Working #Contextual

# Working Memory

## What temporary context is needed to continue or resume this work?

This folder holds records of unfinished work, so another session can pick it up.

## Axioms

- Check these Entries before deciding that no Working record applies. At the start or resume of a task, read the record of that work if there is one, and check it against the current files.

- Keep each record small, current and easy to replace: the goal, where it stands, the next step and open questions.
- An explicitly accepted temporary choice may stay here when its source, scope and expected expiration are clear.
- When the active need ends, keep useful results where they belong, then move, consolidate or prune the record.

## `route update <source-reference>`

Patch one existing source's selected metadata or complete its eligible empty body. Supply at least one operation.

Accepts `--description`, `--responsibility`, repeated `--tag`, repeated `--apply-to`, `--template`, `--clear-apply-to`, and `--dry-run`.

Repeated `--tag` replaces the complete ordered tag list, and `--apply-to` replaces the complete local condition list. `--clear-apply-to` removes local declarations from both supported locations and cannot be combined with `--apply-to`. An exact empty responsibility removes the field, while whitespace-only text is invalid.

`--template` fills an empty or whitespace-only body. Existing authored bodies stay intact with a warning. Source identity, document form, and overwrite ownership remain intact.

## `route move <source-reference> <destination-target>`

Relocate an unmanaged routed leaf or complete category, updating affected references and generated navigation. The destination is an exact workspace-relative `./...` path under an existing routable parent in the context folder, native Skills or the same registered outside route, and must match the source's leaf or category form.

Its only command flag is `--dry-run`. Inspect the move and all reference changes. Move does not relocate lifecycle-managed content, create a missing parent route, or overwrite a destination.

Moving the context folder of an established installation is not available yet. Route Move changes content within the existing layout.

## `route remove <source-reference>`

Remove one routed file or category, record the persistent exclusion, release selected claims, detach references, and update navigation.

Eligible Framework- and Extension-managed content can be removed, including edited files. A category selection removes its whole routed category, including native and binary resources. The loader and `.agents` root stay protected. A native Skill or non-Markdown resource is not a removable routed leaf. Links, incomplete scans, unsafe references, and nested Git repositories block category removal.

- `--dry-run`: inspect dependents, deletions, exclusions, and ownership changes.
- `--automatic`: apply the reviewed plan without confirmation.

## `index [<source-reference>...]`

Index encodes local link paths, such as `old%20guide.md`.
Doctor also accepts readable paths: `<old guide.md>` and `café(one).md`.
Escape an entity-opening ampersand as `%26`: write `entity&.md` as

Repair writes Index's form when
correcting other spellings. Command arguments use literal source paths.
Images with invalid heading fragments need a manual edit.

Complete missing metadata and navigation after manual edits. You may create user-owned Markdown files directly inside routed folders without writing frontmatter or Entries. Index adds missing descriptions from the first heading, otherwise the file name, and the category's tags. It keeps bodies and supplied values. For deep notes below an existing root, it creates every missing entrypoint with metadata and direct-child Entries. Refine the prefilled values later if needed.

An entrypoint selects its subtree and direct exposing parent. A leaf includes its missing chain and direct exposing parent. No operands selects the loader and every eligible rooted entrypoint region, including missing chains. Index removes old entries and adds new ones after renames or moves. When Git retains the old file's committed content, Index and Repair work in either order. Without Git, run Repair first while old Entries still record the file's metadata.

Its only command flag is `--dry-run`. Preview a narrow rebuild before applying it:

```sh
open-forge index memory/crystallized --dry-run
open-forge index memory/crystallized
```

For an Install Git-ignore route, Index uses the policy recorded in `.agents/open-forge.lock.json` to omit private child files and nested private entrypoints from shareable `Entries`. It still maintains the whitelisted route entrypoint and its parent link. This keeps the route available to the team without publishing local private navigation. Overwrites, managed authored content, excluded paths, and recorded private contents are not completed. Index never invents a root or clears an exclusion. Invalid frontmatter stays untouched with an edit instruction, while independent valid files are indexed.

## `repair`

Correct supported local-link issues or recover an incomplete Library operation when current evidence proves the correction safe.

| Flag                                                              | Meaning                                                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--dry-run`                                                       | Preview the complete selected repair plan                                                               |
| `--automatic`                                                     | Select currently verified safe corrections. Guided choices remain unselected                            |
| `--relink <source-location> <expected-destination> <target-path>` | Select one exact current reference occurrence and its contained destination. Repeat for more selections |

Use Doctor to choose a reported target. A relink source location has the form `path@line:column`, with one-based numbers at the start of the link destination. Doctor's displayed location points to the link and cannot be copied directly as a relink location. Inspect the current source, or use Repair's reported destination location, before constructing the request. The expected destination is the exact current authored value, and the target must be an admitted reported candidate.

# Open Forge CLI

Use the optional CLI to read and maintain Open Forge's Markdown, rules, and links. Read this guide before running commands other than `context`. Reading it grants no installation or package-change authority.

First installation can select the context folder with `install --main-root <folder>`. The default is `--main-root .agents`. Native Skills stay in `.agents/skills/`, and settings and ownership stay in `.agents/open-forge.json` and `.agents/open-forge.lock.json`. Use `./...` for exact workspace-relative operands and source IDs for layout-independent selections. Older CLIs do not support custom roots. Relocating an established installation is not available yet. Read [installation details](references/packages.md#install) before an authorized setup change.

Before you write workspace files or metadata, read the file formats in `.agents/README.md`, or run `open-forge help concepts` if that page was deleted.

Folder `route include` registers a maintained outside directory in settings v5. File Include stays read-only by itself. Use exact `./...` source references with filenames outside primary content, and do not infer loading, ownership or package permission from registration. Read [outside-route maintenance](references/routes.md#outside-routes) before editing that content. Older CLIs do not maintain directory registrations, and unknown-property preservation is not downgrade compatibility.

You may create or move user-owned Markdown files directly inside routed folders. Preview and run `open-forge index` to fill missing metadata, create missing entrypoints, and refresh Entries instead of writing those by hand. After renames or moves, preview and run `open-forge repair --automatic` to repair proven links and affected navigation. When Git retains the old file's committed content, Index and Repair work in either order. Without Git, run Repair first while old Entries still record the file's metadata. Index and Repair preserve protected content, including managed files. Follow Doctor's next step for remaining choices, edits or a Git timeout retry. Read [route maintenance](references/routes.md) for the boundaries.

## Most Important Commands

| Need                                              | Start here                             |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Load startup and selected route chains            | `context`                              |
| Find related material by consistent tags          | `find --tag <tag>`                     |
| Discover source IDs and route behavior            | `route list`, `route inspect`          |
| Inspect incoming impact and outgoing dependencies | `references --direction in\|out\|both` |
| Check health and diagnose problems                | `status`, `doctor`                     |
| Preview generated navigation after manual edits   | `index --dry-run`                      |

Check `open-forge --help` once for availability and groups. Use `open-forge <command> --help` for the installed version's exact syntax. If unavailable, follow the loader and maintain the files directly.

Use `open-forge help concepts` for built-in explanations and the file formats from the shipped `.agents/README.md`. It needs no workspace.

Prefer one context request over separate reads for each entrypoint:

```sh
open-forge context --for src/Order.cs --for web/order.ts
```

Supply all known working files, including planned files. Reading a source for context does not make it a working file. Omit `--for` while files are unknown, but resolve pending `applyTo` conditions before relying on those rules. Each applicable source needs one supplied path that matches its complete inherited condition chain. A path filter does not select an unexposed scope or grant edit permission.

Select relevant scopes from returned descriptions and batch their source IDs. After startup is loaded, use `context <selected-source> --additions-only` to omit that startup set. Read returned instructions and obey explicit required-read links too. The CLI follows loading tags, not prose instructions.

## Read Details When Needed

- [Reading and discovery](references/discovery.md): context, tags, headings, direct references, route inspection, and health checks. Find candidates, inspect their relationships, then load only the relevant chain or bounded linked context.
- [Route maintenance](references/routes.md): create, update, move, remove, index, repair, and cleanup. Read before changing routes or generated navigation.
- [Framework and packages](references/packages.md): install setup, update, removal, all Extension commands, and all Library commands. Read for an authorized lifecycle task.
- [Shared options and results](references/common.md): global flags, source syntax, worktrees and sandboxes, previews, unattended execution, permission boundaries, and exit codes. Read before an unfamiliar command or when interpreting a result.

Preview each mutation with `--dry-run` and inspect its plan before applying. Run installation or package changes only when requested. `--automatic`, `--force`, and `--allow-path` add no human authorization. Check semantic status and exit code. Writing commands keep locks and new recovery bundles in the workspace's fixed `.open-forge-state/` folder. Read the worktree and sandbox rules in [shared options and results](references/common.md#worktrees-and-sandboxes) before diagnosing a lock failure. Resolve an in-scope suggested next step or report the boundary when a command is incomplete or blocked. Do not force the same effect through manual edits.

# Open Forge Loader

Agents read this file before every task. It says what to read, how to use it, and how to change what agents use.

The list under `Entries` at the bottom is the whole setup: the folders of rules and notes, and any other documents, that agents use in this workspace. Anything not listed is only background reading. Your project's own requirements, and the instructions your agent tool already loads, still apply. Everything works with plain files, and the CLI only makes it faster.

## Axioms

### Read before you work

1. **List your working files.** Do this when a task starts or resumes, and again after your context is restored. Working files are the files you will investigate, review, create, change, rename or delete, including planned files and both paths of a rename. A file you only read for background is not a working file.
2. **Use the CLI if you can.** If the `open-forge` CLI is available and allowed, run `open-forge context` with `--for <file>` once for each working file, and read its output. It covers steps 3 and 4. You still do step 5 yourself. If the command is missing, fails or cannot follow a link, do steps 3 to 5 with your own file tools.
3. **Check conditions first.** Some entries end with `applies to` and one or more patterns. Such an entry applies only when one of your working files matches it, and that same file also matches every conditioned catalogue above it. Within one list, any pattern may match. Patterns are case-sensitive globs from the workspace root: `*.py` matches root files, `**/*.py` matches any depth, and `docs/**` matches a folder's contents. A leading `!` is literal, not an exclusion. Conditions never open a branch on their own and never grant edit permission. If you don't know your working files yet, report conditioned required entries as pending, and resolve them before you touch a matching file.
4. **Read what is required.** Read every applicable entry tagged #LoadNow or #KeepInMind, in the order listed. A catalogue is a file that lists a folder's context under its own `Entries`. When you read one, repeat steps 3 and 4 for its Entries. Never skip a required read because its description looks unrelated. Read each file once per pass.
5. **Open what fits the task.** Check the descriptions of the other listed entries and open the ones that fit. Follow any link that a file you read says to read. If search or a direct link leads you to a listed file, read the catalogues above it before you apply it. Keep separately selected branches separate. Use catalogues to find things, and don't open ordinary files just to discover more links or tags.

Start again from step 1 when your goal or working files change. Before you hand off or finish, reread the #KeepInMind entries in the branches you are using. During work, reread them only when they may have changed.

### Use what you read

- **Rules.** Follow the `## Axioms` of every catalogue you load and the `## Instructions` of every rule file, within the scope each one states. Only this loader and loaded catalogues define Axioms. A narrower rule adds to a broader one and never outranks it. If two rules conflict, or you cannot follow one, say so and explain why.
- **The user.** Follow the user's direction within platform and safety limits. Take routine, reversible steps inside the request without asking again, and state the assumptions that affect the result. Ask first when an open choice could significantly change the result, scope, risk, cost, external effects or the ability to undo the work.
- **Answers.** Match explanation and planning to the request. Unless the user asks for deeper analysis, start with your current understanding, one recommendation and at most one important open choice.
- **Words.** In replies and in what you write, use the fewest words that keep the meaning, readability and logical order. Cut filler and repetition, but keep the context, conditions and exceptions a reader needs to apply the result.
- **What counts as accepted.** Reading, linking, saving or tagging something does not make it accepted, and does not give you permission to edit it. Content is accepted when the user agrees, or when a source the user named for that question says so. Use declared external authorities for the facts they own. #Contextual marks content that is not accepted, and #CurrentTruth marks accepted current state within its scope. Tags, repetition and your own confidence never make something accepted. Evidence can support a claim without making it accepted.
- **One question per source.** Let each source answer one clear question, and link to related sources instead of repeating their detail. A link never changes either source's authority, scope, loading or lifecycle. Selected advice or other non-binding material may specialize broader material of the same kind within its accepted scope.
- **Conflicts and change.** When two accepted sources disagree, investigate before you edit either. When accepted direction changes the current state, update the source that defines it and keep useful prior context.
- **#Evergreen.** This tag marks material that must stay in step with accepted current state. It grants no authority and loads nothing. Update affected #Evergreen sources you may edit before other work depends on them, and by closeout at the latest. Batch related updates when that is safe.
- **Staying current.** Keep each source true to what it represents now. Keep useful prior context in a listed Memory route or another existing source. Report updates you could not make or were not allowed to make.

### Change what agents use

- **Add something.** Add a line under `Entries` with a path relative to this file, such as `../docs/architecture.md` or `../.cursor/rules/testing.mdc`. The line carries the description, tags and conditions, so the document needs no frontmatter and stays where it is. A linked Markdown catalogue, such as `../docs/_docs.md`, brings its Entries along. With the CLI, `open-forge route include <file>` writes the line for you.
- **Remove something.** Remove its line. Its files stay as plain notes, and reading them for background does not bring their rules back. Removing a line does not cancel accepted project requirements or the instructions your agent tool loads on its own. A removed line stays removed until the user asks to restore it.
- **Check what depends on it.** Before you remove a line, remove or replace the listed parts that need it, and report anything you cannot resolve. Inside other catalogues, the list follows the files in that folder, so move or delete a file to keep it out. When the CLI manages updates, also record the removal in its exclusions before you update.
- **Missing files.** Report a listed file or required dependency that is missing as an error. An empty `Entries` list is valid.
- **Required reads.** #LoadNow means a file is read whenever its parent loads. #KeepInMind adds the rereads described above. Both act only through catalogues you have read, so neither opens a branch nobody selected. Keep a required file's catalogue chain unbroken. Add these tags only when the read is really needed, and narrow specialized content before you make it required. No other tag changes loading.
- **Writing context.** Before you author workspace context, catalogues or metadata, read the file formats under "Writing workspace files" in `README.md`. If that page was deleted, `open-forge help concepts` prints the same section. Without either, copy the shape of a neighbouring file. New routed files carry `description`, `tags` and optional `applyTo`. A native `SKILL.md` keeps its own metadata.
- **Changes that survive updates.** Put your change in `{name}.overwrite.md` next to the shipped file. It is read right after its base, with the same role, scope and loading conditions. It wins only where the two say different things about the same content, and it is not listed or selected on its own.

## Entries

- [Required instructions loaded through selected routes](directives/_directives.md) - #LoadNow #Core #Directive

# Memory

## What is worth remembering for current or future work?

Memory is self-growing Markdown state: people and agents add useful records and routed scopes without a fixed structural limit. A record need not pass through every state.

## Axioms

### What to keep

- Save agent communication and coordination only when they must survive the current context. Do not save every conversation.
- Save a durable outcome when future work needs the accepted result, its reasoning, a required behavior or a reusable shape. Otherwise create no durable record. Before closeout, also keep unsettled findings worth revisiting.
- Show where a record came from and how certain it is when that affects trust or later acceptance. Distinguish what was stated, observed or inferred.
- Update affected sources before other work depends on the outcome and no later than closeout. Keep useful context and reasoning in Memory. Accepted durable knowledge must reach the source that defines it, not stay only in chat or an unaccepted record.

### Where it goes

- An accepted record can define current knowledge. Recording another category's content does not give the record that category's role. Saving or moving a record does not make it accepted.
- Add records and routed scopes when their likely future value justifies the cost of finding and reviewing them. Use an existing suitable record before creating another.
- Move material when its state, scope or intended use changes, and leave no stale or competing copy. The destination's rules govern its new role. Put accepted instructions for future agent behavior in the source for that role.
- A record needs no named category. Use an existing state and the narrowest useful scope. Do not recreate a removed folder merely to save a record.
- Within the authority granted for the work, add an ordinary record or scoped route when needed. Ask when placement would change accepted meaning or cross an unresolved authority boundary. Get explicit user direction before creating a new top-level Memory state.

## Entries

- [Useful history that no longer controls current work](archived/_archived.md) - #Memory #Archived #Contextual #Historical
- [Accepted knowledge that should remain current](crystallized/_crystallized.md) - #LoadNow #Memory #Crystallized #CurrentTruth
- [Useful material that is not accepted yet](emerging/_emerging.md) - #KeepInMind #Memory #Emerging #Contextual #Candidate
- [Temporary memory that helps agents continue or resume active work](working/_working.md) - #LoadNow #Memory #Working #Contextual

## What temporary context is needed to continue or resume this work?

# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](technology/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](technology/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Neon Pairs

Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every matching pair. Read the [game specification and document map](docs/README.md) for gameplay and implementation requirements.

## Build and run

The game uses React, TypeScript and Vite. Dependencies and versions are pinned in `package-lock.json`.

```sh
npm ci
npm run dev
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run test:e2e
npm run build
npm run --silent replay -- PATH
```

`npm run test:e2e` builds from current source before starting Playwright. The build failure stops the browser run. `npm run build` emits the standalone offline distribution at [dist/index.html](dist/index.html); open it directly from disk to play.

## Verification

The tested compatibility combination was Node.js `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0`, Playwright `1.64.1` and Chromium `156.0.8078.4`.

- `npm ci` installed 50 packages; audit reported zero vulnerabilities.
- `npm run typecheck` passed.
- `npm test` passed 18 unit tests in 4 files.
- `npm run test:e2e` built the distribution and passed 33 browser journeys in 4.9 minutes.
- `npm run build` passed and emitted `dist/index.html` at 242,007 bytes (242.00 kB).
- A post-split focused run passed all 6 keyboard/accessibility and touch browser journeys.
- After the final snapshot-editor typography adjustment, typecheck/build passed again and the affected control browser journey passed 1/1.
- The valid replay example exited 0, wrote only its final snapshot to stdout and left stderr empty. Invalid `{}` exited 1, left stdout empty and wrote `Invalid replay.` to stderr.
- `npm run dev` served the game at a local HTTP URL; a request returned `<title>Neon Pairs</title>`. The server was stopped after the check.
- Browser tests opened the built file from `file://` with network access disabled. The single HTML file made no network requests. Local HTTP tests confirmed saved size persistence and continued play when storage operations throw.

The automated accessibility journey records the initial board, first reveal, completed game and keyboard reset: [accessibility journey](evidence/accessibility-journey.txt). It was captured with Playwright `1.64.1` and Chromium `156.0.8078.4`. No screen reader was used; spoken output and real-device touch long-press remain user-acceptance checks from the specification.

The [grayscale face sheet](evidence/grayscale-faces.png) shows all 128 identities at 44px on a completed 16x16 board. The sheet was generated with grayscale artwork, then visually reviewed for shape, marker direction and solid/outline differences.

Read the complete [acceptance journeys](docs/acceptance.md) and [architecture](docs/technology/architecture.md).
